guest.bio_context: Christopher Mims is a tech reporter at the Wall Street Journal and author of two books: 'How to AI: Cut Through the Hype, Master the Basics, Transform Your Work' and 'Arriving Today: From Factory to Front Door, Why Everything Has Changed About How and What We Buy.' He has spent time with Colin Angle, the founder of iRobot, and has observed developments in robotics and AI innovation across multiple countries including China.

pending_qa.q: Why is a humanoid robot design preferred over specialized robots for specific tasks?
pending_qa.r: The world is already made for humans, so if you want to automate what people do, you need something roughly shaped like a human with the same reach. A humanoid robot can be sold to many more customers because it can flip burgers in any restaurant, operate in Amazon warehouses with flexibility, and adapt to many different situations, whereas a customized robot only works for one specific task.

pending_qa.q: What makes laundry folding such a difficult task for humanoid robots compared to other warehouse tasks?
pending_qa.r: Robots love repetitive tasks and rigid surfaces, but an average T-shirt is a wobbly noodle of a thing that requires real hard thinking about where to grab it. While robots have solved picking things out of bins and sealing boxes, getting a robot to pick up a shirt and fold it acceptably or sort through a bin of laundry turns out to be a really hard problem because of all the variability involved.

pending_qa.q: How does Aptronic's approach to humanoid robot development differ from traditional methods?
pending_qa.r: Aptronic, based in Austin Texas, is trying to build the cheapest, best humanoid robot but intentionally kept it totally mindless. Their CEO says they are just trying to make the best robot body and leave the brains to other people, with their partner being Google's DeepMind, which develops novel kinds of AI to drive robot bodies.

pending_qa.q: What is Moravec's paradox and how does it relate to current advances in robotics and AI?
pending_qa.r: Moravec's paradox states that it is easier to teach a humanoid robot to beat a human at chess than it is to teach it to pick up and move the pieces on a physical chessboard. For 50 to 100 years this has been true, but new kinds of AI different from today's chatbots are enabling new flexibility in robot behavior such that robots can finally be animated in ways that weren't possible before.

pending_qa.q: How do Chinese AI companies approach model distribution differently than U.S. companies?
pending_qa.r: China does open weights models, which means you can download them and use them any way you want, whereas in the U.S. you have to pay for these services. Chinese companies have recognized they may not be able to compete head to head with U.S. companies that have seemingly unlimited resources for giant supercomputers, so they work smarter by leveraging their resources and sharing the AIs they create with the world.

pending_qa.q: What role did government loans play in enabling Tesla's domestic manufacturing success?
pending_qa.r: Tesla would not be here today without multi-hundred million dollar loans from the U.S. Department of Energy, which wanted to support the manufacturer domestically of electric vehicles. This is called industrial policy, and China is great at it with its five-year plans that explicitly state what the country will prioritize and pour money into.

pending_qa.q: What does the future moonshot in the AI and robotics race look like according to technology experts?
pending_qa.r: Landing on the moon in this technological race means the first time you walk into a workplace, a restaurant, an office, and there is a robot standing there doing a job and no one finds it remarkable. This would represent the normalization of robots in everyday human spaces.
